lines.note: Tokiwa and tokiwana describe something unchanging. The capital T and following oqiua are visible; the initial OCR fro- does not belong to the printed headword.

runs.text: ou ſẽpre eſtà no meſmo ſer. ¶

lines.note: The gloss continues with remaining always in the same condition. The repeated adjective starts at the right and is divided after Toqiua-.

runs.text: Homẽ q̃ parece ſẽpre està no meſmo

lines.note: Na hito completes tokiwana hito, a person who appears always to remain the same. The Portuguese sentence continues into the explanation of aging and consistency below.

runs.text: ſer ſem enuelhecer, ou q̃ não faz mudança

lines.note: The person remains unchanged without growing old, or does not change his intentions and habits. Preserve the printed enuelhecer spelling and the abbreviation q̃.
Completes the second application of tokiwana hito: constancy in purposes and customs. Cuſtumes is the printed historical form, not silently modernized to costumes.

runs.text: P. Modo de caſas, ou edi-

lines.note: Tokiwa kakiwa is labeled poetic and describes a configuration of houses or buildings. The narrow printed separation between the two Japanese forms is retained; the Portuguese edi- continues as edificios on the following row.
Completes edificios: the buildings are closely joined together. This explains the preceding compound rather than beginning another headword.
Tokiwagi denotes evergreen trees. The Portuguese ſempre has long s, not the OCR f; the following line explains the persistence of their leaves.
The trees never lose their foliage, completing the evergreen definition. The initial n of nunca is visible and corrects OCR munca; cae remains the historical spelling.
Tokiyo is the current time or age. A capital T is printed, not F; the repeated To- begins an example extending onto the next row.
Tokiyo ni shitagōte means according to the time or age. The caron over o is retained in the historical contracted form xitagǒte.
Completes the gloss with age or era. The short continuation belongs to the example above and remains a separate physical line.
Tokiyurushi, with the abbreviated inflected forms, means untying and releasing. The Portuguese verbs express loosening a bond, consistent with toki- and yurusu.

runs.text: O determinar, ou limitar a hora

lines.note: Tokizashi means fixing or specifying an hour. The initial capital is T; the Portuguese construction continues with the purpose for which the time is set.
The appointed time is for some activity. Tokizashi wo shite mai- begins the example of going at a fixed time; mairu continues on the next line.

runs.text: Ir determinando a hora, ou tempo.

lines.note: Ru completes mairu. The Portuguese paraphrase is going with the hour or time specified, rather than a second independent verb entry.

runs.text: O eſcreuer a hora como em que ſe

lines.note: Tokizuke denotes writing down the time. The explanation begins a comparison with noting when a letter is dispatched or an event occurs.

runs.text: manda a carta, ou aconteceo algũa couſa no-

lines.note: Continues with sending a letter or the occurrence of a notable event. The printed no- is the first part of notauel, not the Japanese particle no.
Completes notauel and gives tokizuke wo suru, making such a time notation. Vt is the italic example introducer, while the Japanese phrase remains roman.
Tōka is explained by momo no hana, peach blossom. The scan clearly has Flor, including the small l missed by OCR; the headword carries a caron.
Tōka with the printed circumflex is equated with tomoshibi, lamplight. The oil-lamp explanation continues below and distinguishes it from the peach-blossom entry above.
Azeite completes candea de azeite, an oil lamp. It is the final word of the preceding definition.
Tora is the ordinary word for a tiger, directly glossed by Portuguese tigre. The following separate entry gives its calendrical use.

runs.text: Hum dos animaes, ou ſignos celestes por

lines.note: Tora here names the Tiger among the zodiacal animals or signs. The scan has a capital T, not the lowercase OCR r, and the explanation continues below.

runs.text: onde os Iapões contão as horas, ou annos.

lines.note: The Japanese count hours and years using these animal signs. This is the indented continuation of the Tiger entry, not an unindented new entry.
Tora no koku is the Tiger hour, glossed here as four or five hours after midnight. Preserve the dictionary's stated time rather than harmonizing it to another timekeeping system.
Completes the time reference with after midnight. Mea noite is the printed phrase and is retained as two words.
Torakashi, torakasu means dissolving or melting something. Wax supplies the first example, and further material and figurative uses follow.
Lead completes the list of things melted. Hito wo torakasu then extends the verb to a person, with the following gloss explaining the figurative softening.

Hito no kokoro wo torakasu elaborates softening someone's heart. The third letter of Fitono is abraded, but its lower curved foot agrees with the t in Fitouo directly above rather than the r in toracaſu; retain this damaged-glyph caveat. Cocorouo contains the object marker, and Abrandar begins its translation.

runs.text: o coração dalguem que estaua duro, & tornalo

lines.note: Abrandar governs the heart of someone who had been hard, making it pliable. Preserve the historical estaua and tornalo spellings and the aligned short-s form.
The heart becomes like melted wax. The next example begins with meat or fish; the abraded vowel after N is read as i in Nicu, supported by the surviving foot and the following carne translation.

runs.text: Cozer carne, ou peixe de ma-

lines.note: Ni torakasu describes cooking meat or fish until soft. Ma- begins maneira, the Portuguese phrase describing how thoroughly it is cooked.
Completes maneira and explains that the food becomes dissolved and broken down. The printing's short s in desfeito is retained.
Torage names a tiger's colour or coat. The divided To- begins examples applying the coat pattern to domestic animals.
Torage inu and torage neko are a tiger-patterned dog or cat. Latin l introduces the second alternative and is not Japanese text.
The dog or cat is patterned like a tiger. This completes the animal-coat examples, without requiring a modern distinction between stripes and mottling.
Tōrai is explained by itari, kitaru and by coming or arriving. The printed caron is visible and the entry concerns arrival rather than the following homonymous meanings.
Jikoku tōrai suru means that the time arrives. Initial Ii has the consonantal reading ji; the worn lower-case t in tǒrai and separated ou vir correct OCR fǒrai and ourvir.

runs.text: tempo, & hora de fazer algũa couſa.

lines.note: The time and hour for doing something arrive. This is the continuation of chegarſe, ou vir above and closes the arrival entry.
This tōrai means news. Tōrai ga aru or gozaru illustrates having or receiving news; the final go- continues on the next row.
Zaru completes gozaru, and the Portuguese means that there is news or that news arrives. Nouas corrects the OCR nonas; the upright X. is a regional usage label.
A third tōrai is equated with raise, the world to come. The Portuguese Mundo has an abraded u but is supported by the surviving shape and the explanation, not OCR Mando.
Tro completes outro, giving the alternative other world. The text continues the eschatological definition and is not a separate entry.

runs.text: Couſa malhada, ou de cor de ti-

lines.note: Toramadara describes something patterned or coloured like a tiger. The Portuguese ti- continues into tigre on the next row.

The example concerns a puppy with a tiger-like coat. The final part of expected Toramadara is badly abraded: only a dot-like remnant is secure after Toramadar, so Toramadar. no is retained without supplying the missing a. Cachor- continues as cachorrinho below.
Rinho completes cachorrinho, a little dog patterned like a tiger. Enlargement recovers malhado como tigre from the damaged OCR sequence; the physical line is retained.
Toramaye means seizing or taking hold. The italic Meliùs recommends Torayuru as the preferable form; this is an alternative lexical form, and the next row supplies its Portuguese meaning.
Completes toramaye: taking hold or grasping. The phrase ter mão refers to getting a grip rather than merely possessing a hand.
Tora no o is identified only as a kind of herb. The gloss does not justify choosing a particular modern botanical species.
Torake is the intransitive counterpart of melting or dissolving. The reflexive Portuguese infinitives agree with that sense; co- continues into como.

runs.text: mo chumbo, cera, peixe muito cozido, &c.

lines.note: Completes como and gives lead, wax, and thoroughly cooked fish as things that soften or dissolve. These examples parallel the transitive torakashi entry in column 1.
Sake ni kokoro ga torakuru illustrates the heart softening through wine. The italic Per met. marks the figurative extension and is visibly separated into two parts.

runs.text: Abrandarſe, & mouerſe de todo pera algũa

lines.note: The heart softens and is wholly moved toward something. This begins the Portuguese explanation of the wine example and continues onto the next row.

runs.text: couſa o coração do homem com vinho.

lines.note: Completes the statement that wine moves a person's heart toward something. The line belongs to the same figurative example, not a new definition.

runs.text: Cor de caualo malhado como ti-

lines.note: Toratsukige names a horse colour or coat pattern likened to a tiger. The Portuguese ti- continues across the physical line boundary.
Completes tigre and gives toratsukige no uma, a horse with that coat. The example is standalone Japanese rather than a word embedded in Portuguese prose.
Toraware means being taken prisoner or captive. The dictionary gives the passive verb's principal forms and continues by specifying wartime capture.
In war completes the captive definition. The short line is a physical continuation of toraware.
Torawarebito is a captive or someone taken by enemies. Catiuo has u rather than the OCR n in Catino.
Torase means giving to a socially inferior person. The Portuguese marks the direction of the social relation rather than describing an intrinsically inferior gift.
Toraye means seizing, taking prisoner, or laying hold of someone. The third Portuguese expression continues on the following row.

Lançar mão dalguem completes the seizure definition. The separate far-right ( and ou toma. are printed on this same physical row but complete the next entry's lugar por onde ſe afferra, ou toma; they are retained in place rather than moved into its text line.
Toraedokoro is a place by which something can be grasped. The comma links it semantically to the displaced ou toma. printed at the far right of the preceding row.
Tore is a nautical verb for the wind abating or ceasing. Ven- begins vento, continued on the next row.
Completes vento and explicitly identifies sailors' vocabulary. Kaze ga introduces the example whose verb appears below.
Kaze ga toreta means the wind stopped. Ceßou is the printed Portuguese past tense, with its double-s sort retained.
A second tore is described as the passive of Tori, u, to take. The referenced Japanese form is roman throughout; the printed abbreviated u is retained without supplying an expected r.
Uo ga ōku toreta means that many fish were caught. The historical vouoqu spelling is retained; Tomou- is entirely italic and continues into the next row.
Completes tomou-se muito peixe, much fish was caught. The scan includes the i in peixe and shows the continuation at the normal indentation.
Tori is a bird, directly glossed by pássaro in the printed spelling Paßaro. This short entry is distinct from the following Sino-Japanese homonym.
Tōri names peach and plum, explained by momo and sumomo. The mark above o is a downward caron, correcting the provisional circumflex; a- begins the second Portuguese tree name.
Meixieira completes ameixieira, the plum tree. The separate upright S. marks written-language usage and is not part of the italic tree name.

runs.text: Hum dos animaes por onde contão os Ia-

lines.note: Tori here names the Bird or Rooster zodiacal sign by which the Japanese count time. The scan supplies the t in contão missed by OCR; Ia- continues into Iapões.
Completes the statement about counting hours and years. Tori no koku introduces the particular time associated with the Bird sign.

runs.text: As 6. ou 7. horas depois do meo dia.

lines.note: The dictionary gives the Bird hour as six or seven hours after midday. Preserve its explicit reckoning and printed meo dia wording rather than substituting a modern conversion.
Tori, toru, totta means taking or catching. Tori wo toru supplies the first example, catching birds, and is translated on the next line.

runs.text: Tomar paßaros com viſco, ou com rede, &c.

lines.note: Birds are caught with birdlime or a net. Tomar belongs wholly to the italic Portuguese gloss; its capital does not create a separate Japanese T.
Kubi wo toru means taking a head in warfare. The Portuguese gloss explains this martial use of the general taking verb.
Na wo toru means gaining a name or reputation. The meaning is acquiring fame rather than physically taking someone's name.
Yado wo toru is taking lodgings or renting a house. The whole Portuguese Tomar is italic; the OCR split off its capital incorrectly.
Shoryō wo toru refers to acquiring an estate or its income, which the Portuguese renders as obtaining revenue. The caron in the Japanese form is retained.
Ta no me wo toru is taking another man's wife. The printed Portuguese describes stealing another's wife; a- continues into alhea.
Lhea completes alhea. Te wo torikumu then begins the example about interlocking or taking one another's hands, with its Portuguese explanation continued below.

runs.text: ſi as mãos como quem luta, &c. ¶

lines.note: The hands are taken together as when wrestling. Cuji- begins the next example, drawing lots; the line break is preserved in the Japanese phrase.
Kuji wo toru means drawing or casting lots. Enlargement resolves Deitar, whose joined i and t caused OCR Deuar; Momodachi- begins the clothing example on the next row.
Momodachi wo toru means tucking up the lower garment. The Portuguese describes raising the breeches and placing their ends somewhere, completed in the next line.
The garment ends are tucked into the belt. Chi wo toru introduces bloodletting, and the Portuguese San- continues into sangrar.

runs.text: grar: particularmente ſe diz de caualos. ¶

lines.note: Completes sangrar and specifies that the expression is especially used of horses. Te starts the next example about instruction by taking a learner's hand.
Te wo totte oshiyuru means teaching by taking someone's hand. Voxiyuru retains the dictionary's historical form; the Portuguese identifies the recipient as a learner.
The teacher takes and guides the learner's hand. Aca- begins the next example referring to bilge water, not the colour red in this context.
Aka wo toru means working the pump to remove bilge water. Mi wo toru then introduces gathering fruit; the worn u of Miuo corrects the OCR t in Mito.

runs.text: Tomar, ou recolher fruito dos campos, ou das

lines.note: Mi wo toru means taking or gathering produce from fields or trees. The abraded opening ou is read from the surviving curved remnant and syntax; recolher corrects the OCR vowel, while the printed fruito spelling is retained.
Trees completes the literal gathering-fruit sense. Itẽ, per met. introduces a figurative use of mi wo toru that continues onto the following page, anticipated by the catchword Tirar.
